diagrams.name: emerg-p408-vasoconstriction
diagrams.title: Cold vs heat on blood vessels

cloze.text: In cardiac arrest, open the airway and give rescue breaths only if you are {{c1::trained and equipped}}.
In cardiac arrest, use the {{c1::AED}} as soon as possible and follow its voice prompts.
Continue CPR until {{c1::emergency help arrives}} or {{c2::the patient recovers}}.
Using an AED within the first {{c1::3–5 minutes}} of cardiac arrest can raise survival rates to over {{c2::70%}}.
cloze.extra: Did you know: the first portable AED was invented in the 1970s, but AEDs only became common in public places in the 1990s.

cloze.text: Severe hypoglycemia is called {{c1::insulin shock}}.
Hyperglycemia = blood glucose above {{c1::130}} mg/dL fasting or above {{c2::180}} mg/dL post-meal.
Causes of hypoglycemia: skipping {{c1::meals}}, taking diabetes meds, {{c2::alcohol}}, and {{c3::physical exertion}}.
Causes of hyperglycemia: {{c1::skipped diabetes meds}}, too many {{c2::carbs}}, stress, and {{c3::infection}}.
Diabetic coma is caused by {{c1::severe insulin shock (severe hypoglycemia)}} or {{c2::diabetic ketoacidosis}}.
Hypoglycemia signs: dizziness, sweating, shakiness, confusion, headache, rapid heart rate, and especially {{c1::moodiness and hunger}}; it may lead to {{c2::seizures or unconsciousness}}.
Hyperglycemia signs: nausea, thirst, {{c1::fruity breath}}, fatigue, confusion, and {{c2::frequent urination}}.
A patient in diabetic coma is {{c1::unresponsive}} and may first show signs of either hypo- or hyperglycemia.
Hypoglycemia management: give 15 g glucose every {{c1::15 minutes}}; {{c2::juice or candy}} is OK.
Unconscious hypoglycemic patient: give {{c1::1 mg glucagon IM}} and call EMS if needed.
Hyperglycemia management: call EMS if the patient is {{c1::unstable}} or shows signs of {{c2::ketoacidosis}}.
Hypoglycemia improves within {{c1::10–15 minutes}}; have the patient rest {{c2::1 hour}} before discharge.
Schedule diabetic patients' appointments in the {{c1::morning}}, {{c2::after meals}}.
cloze.extra: Diabetes drugs lower blood sugar, so the patient needs a meal to balance blood sugar.

cloze.text: Hyperglycemia may lead to diabetic coma; do NOT {{c1::treat symptomatic (hyperglycemic) patients in the dental chair}}.
In hypoglycemia, there isn't enough circulating glucose to supply energy to tissues, especially the {{c1::brain}}.
Hypoglycemia can result from taking insulin/diabetes meds without eating enough {{c1::carbs}}, using glucose up too quickly (e.g., {{c2::intense exercise}}), or fasting/skipping meals.
Alcohol contributes to hypoglycemia because alcohol metabolism {{c1::blocks glucose release from the liver}}.
Untreated hypoglycemia causes confusion, shakiness, seizures, fainting and, in severe cases, {{c1::coma}}.
In hyperglycemia, glucose builds up in the blood because {{c1::insulin}} is missing or not working properly.
{{c1::Insulin resistance}} (common in Type 2 diabetes) can cause hyperglycemia.

Without effective insulin, cells can't use glucose, so the body breaks down {{c1::fat}} for energy, creating {{c2::ketones}}, which can lead to {{c3::diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)}} — a dangerous acidic condition.
The fruity breath of DKA comes from {{c1::acetone}}, a volatile ketone exhaled through the lungs.
cloze.extra: Smells sweet — like overripe fruit or nail polish remover.

cloze.text: Swallowed fluoride reacts with stomach {{c1::hydrochloric acid}} to form {{c2::hydrofluoric acid}}, which burns the gastric lining.
The gastric burn of fluoride toxicity causes {{c1::GI}} symptoms: nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, diarrhea.
In the blood, fluoride binds {{c1::calcium}}, causing {{c2::hypocalcemia}}.
Fluoride-induced hypocalcemia affects the nervous system: muscle {{c1::tetany}}, paresthesia, seizures and, in severe cases, {{c2::cardiac arrhythmia}}, convulsions or coma.
Fluoride ingestion below 5 mg/kg: give {{c1::milk}} — it protects the stomach lining and binds fluoride to calcium, decreasing absorption.
Substitutes for milk after fluoride ingestion: {{c1::lime water}}, {{c2::antacid}}, or condensed milk.
Fluoride ingestion below 5 mg/kg: also induce vomiting and {{c1::observe the patient for a few hours}}.
Fluoride ingestion of 5–15 mg/kg: activate EMS and admit to hospital; give {{c1::calcium orally}} and {{c2::induce vomiting}}.
Fluoride ingestion of 5–15 mg/kg: the hospital monitors heart, calcium, magnesium, potassium and pH; {{c1::intravenous calcium}} may restore blood calcium.
Fluoride ingestion above {{c1::15}} mg/kg: EMS + hospital; empty the stomach, give {{c2::calcium gluconate IV}}, and monitor for cardiac arrhythmias.
Swallowing a whole {{c1::tube of toothpaste}} can exceed the 5 mg/kg mild-toxicity threshold for a young child.
Fluoride varnish contains just {{c1::5–11 mg}} of fluoride — far below toxic thresholds, even for young children.
Topical anesthetics can cause {{c1::methemoglobinemia}}, in which hemoglobin loses its ability to carry oxygen.
Methemoglobinemia is most often caused by excessive {{c1::benzocaine}} on mucosa, especially in {{c2::children}}.
Methemoglobinemia signs: pale or bluish skin (especially lips), shortness of breath, fatigue, confusion, rapid heart rate, and {{c1::cyanosis that does not improve with oxygen}}.
Methemoglobinemia protocol: stop treatment, call 911, give {{c1::oxygen}} even if cyanosis persists, monitor vitals, and tell EMS methemoglobinemia is suspected.
Hospital treatment of methemoglobinemia may require {{c1::methylene blue}}.
Avoid topical benzocaine on {{c1::infants}} and {{c2::ulcerated tissue}}; use only small, measured amounts.
Local anesthetic toxicity results from overdose, too-rapid injection, or {{c1::injection into a blood vessel}}.
Local anesthetic toxicity affects the {{c1::CNS}} first and may progress to {{c2::cardiovascular collapse}}.
Signs of local anesthetic toxicity include a {{c1::metallic taste}}, {{c2::ringing in the ears}}, numb tongue, dizziness, slurred speech and tremors.
Severe local anesthetic toxicity: {{c1::seizures}}, hypotension, {{c2::bradycardia}}, and potential cardiac arrest.
Local anesthetic toxicity protocol: stop, call 911, place the patient {{c1::supine}}, give {{c2::oxygen}}; if a seizure occurs, protect from injury; be ready for CPR and an AED.
To prevent local anesthetic toxicity, always {{c1::aspirate}} before injecting, stay within safe dose limits, and monitor the patient closely.
The mandible is connected to the temporal bone by {{c1::muscles and ligaments}}.
The mandibular condyle normally sits in the {{c1::glenoid (articular) fossa}} of the temporal bone.
Mandibular dislocation: the condyle moves {{c1::forward}} past the {{c2::articular eminence}} — e.g., when yawning, chewing, or opening for dental procedures.

Reducing a dislocated mandible: brace the patient's head firmly against the {{c1::headrest}}; place the clinician's {{c2::protected thumbs}} on the occlusal surfaces of the mandible, other fingers around the {{c3::ramus}}.
To reduce a dislocated mandible, push it {{c1::down}} first, then guide it {{c2::back}} and {{c3::up}} so the condyle returns into the fossa.
Don't be confused: {{c1::trismus}} = jaw stuck closed or limited opening; {{c2::dislocation}} = jaw stuck open and cannot close.
Bite blocks or mouth props used during lengthy procedures can cause {{c1::mandibular dislocation or trismus}}; instruct patients to gently {{c2::exercise the jaw}} post-procedure.
Trismus is commonly caused by trauma, infection, inflammation, or dental complications such as a {{c1::posterior superior alveolar (PSA)}} nerve block.
In trismus, patients can't open fully, and {{c1::chewing and speaking}} can become painful.
Severe trismus with fever and generalized muscle stiffness can be a sign of {{c1::tetanus}}.
Trismus protocol: apply {{c1::warm}} compresses, recommend gentle jaw-stretching exercises, rest the jaw and avoid wide opening; a {{c2::mouth-opening exercise device}} increases range of motion.
When a tooth is avulsed, the {{c1::periodontal ligament (PDL)}} is torn, but many of its cells may remain alive on the {{c2::root surface}} — essential for reattachment.
Handle an avulsed tooth only by the {{c1::crown}}; do not touch or clean the root.
Gently rinse debris off an avulsed tooth and transport it in liquid; keep the root moist — do not wrap it in {{c1::paper}}.
{{c1::Save-A-Tooth®}} is the best storage medium: its pH (~7.2) and osmolality (280–300 mOsm) match PDL cells, and it contains glucose, Ca²⁺, phosphate and K⁺.
{{c1::Whole milk}} is a good avulsed-tooth storage medium: osmolality similar to root cells, widely available; do NOT use {{c2::skim milk or cream}}.
{{c1::Saline}} is acceptable for storing an avulsed tooth — isotonic and safe for short transport.
Saliva (buccal fold) is not ideal for an avulsed tooth: low osmolality and high {{c1::bacterial content}}.
{{c1::Water or ice}} is a poor storage medium: its very low osmolality (7–17 mOsm) causes {{c2::cell rupture}}.
Never store an avulsed tooth {{c1::dry}} (tissue, glass) — it kills root cells rapidly.
Avulsed permanent tooth: {{c1::replant immediately}} in its original position.
Replantation success depends on the {{c1::vitality of the cells remaining on the root surface}}.
A foreign object in the eye may be {{c1::superficial}} (e.g., dust, eyelash) or {{c2::embedded}} in the surface.
Signs of a foreign body in the eye: discomfort, {{c1::tearing}}, redness, blurry vision, and a feeling of something in the eye.
Foreign body in eye: {{c1::wash your hands}} with soap and water first; use an {{c2::eyewash station}} if available, or flush with clean lukewarm water.
Rinse the eye from the {{c1::inner (medial)}} to the {{c2::outer (lateral)}} corner to avoid cross-contamination.
An {{c1::eyecup or clean glass}} can be positioned against the bone at the base of the eye socket to rinse the eye.
Have the patient remove {{c1::contact lenses}} to access the eye surface more clearly.
Do not attempt to remove {{c1::embedded}} objects or {{c2::rub}} the eye.
Seek emergency care if the object can't be removed or the patient has continued {{c1::pain or visual changes}}; mild redness may persist even after removal.
Initial choking signs in an adult/child: coughing, wheezing, cyanosis, inability to speak, and the {{c1::universal choking sign}}.
Initial choking signs in an infant: {{c1::weak cry}}, ineffective breathing, cyanosis, limpness, choking gesture.
If a choking victim is coughing forcefully, {{c1::let them keep coughing}} — it is the most effective way to clear the airway; do not interfere.
Abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver) are used for conscious choking adults and children over {{c1::1 year}} who cannot breathe.

Heimlich maneuver: stand behind the person, place a fist just above the {{c1::navel}}, grasp it with the other hand, and deliver quick {{c2::inward and upward}} thrusts until the object is expelled or the person becomes unresponsive.
Choking infant: lay the infant {{c1::face-down}} along your forearm, supporting the head and neck, and deliver back blows between the {{c2::shoulder blades}} with the heel of your hand.
Infant chest thrusts: turn the infant face-up, support the head, and press with {{c1::2 fingers}} on the breastbone just below the {{c2::nipple line}}.
If a choking victim becomes unconscious: call 911, lower them to the floor (infant: a firm surface), and begin {{c1::CPR}} if needed.
Opening the airway: adult/child — {{c1::tilt the head back and lift the chin}}; infant — {{c2::neutral head position}}.
cloze.extra: Do NOT tilt an infant's head back — the infant airway is more flexible and narrower.

cloze.text: In any choking victim, do NOT perform a {{c1::blind finger sweep}}; remove an object only if it is clearly visible.
Begin CPR on a choking victim who is unresponsive and {{c1::not breathing}}.
Excessive bleeding can occur during or after NSPT, prophylaxis, periodontal surgery, restorative procedures, or {{c1::extractions}}.
Post-procedure bleeding: apply {{c1::firm pressure with gauze}} until a clot forms.
Conditions associated with increased bleeding risk: anticoagulants, {{c1::antiplatelets}}, and {{c2::NSAIDs}}.
A dental procedure may reveal an undiagnosed bleeding disorder such as {{c1::hemophilia}} or {{c2::von Willebrand's disease}} for the first time.
Dry socket is most common {{c1::1–3 days}} after extraction, especially in {{c2::lower molars}}.
Dry socket risk factors: using a straw, spitting, {{c1::smoking}}, poor oral hygiene, and trauma to the area.
Dry socket treatment: {{c1::irrigation}}, {{c2::medicated dressings}}, and pain relief.
A nosebleed occurs when delicate vessels in the {{c1::nasal lining}} rupture — from dryness, trauma (nose-picking, sneezing), hypertension, or clotting disorders.
Most nosebleeds are {{c1::anterior}} and self-limiting.
Epistaxis: sit upright and lean {{c1::forward}} — this lowers pressure in the nasal veins and prevents {{c2::swallowing blood}}, which irritates the stomach.

Epistaxis: keep the head higher than the {{c1::heart}}, apply a cold compress, put gauze in the nostril, and pinch the nose with thumb and index finger for {{c2::10 minutes}} while breathing through the mouth.
After a nosebleed, advise the patient not to {{c1::touch or blow the nose}} for a few hours.
In dentistry, hematomas most often follow {{c1::local anesthetic injections}}, when the needle traumatizes a vein or artery.
The {{c1::inferior alveolar}} nerve block has a higher chance of hematoma because the needle penetrates deeper into the tissue.
A PSA nerve block can cause a hematoma by puncturing the {{c1::pterygoid venous plexus}} in the {{c2::infratemporal fossa}}.
Hematoma, first day: apply {{c1::ice packs}} a few times a day — vasoconstriction decreases hemorrhage and edema.
Hematoma, from the following day: apply {{c1::heat}} — vasodilation helps resorption of blood; never on the first day.
cloze.extra: The condition should resolve on its own.

basic.front: Which three things should NOT be given during cardiac arrest (per the book)?
basic.back: Nitroglycerin, aspirin, oxygen — they do not help during cardiac arrest.
Unconscious state due to extreme hypo- or hyperglycemia
basic.extra: The brain can no longer function properly; both conditions can lead to permanent brain damage or death.

basic.front: Diabetic emergency and you are unsure whether it is hypo- or hyperglycemia — what do you do, and why?
basic.back: Call EMS immediately and give glucose: it can save a hypoglycemic patient and won't harm a hyperglycemic one short-term.
basic.extra: It is safer to treat as hypoglycemia — hypoglycemic coma can lead to brain damage or death.

basic.front: Why does moodiness or sudden irritability occur in hypoglycemia?
basic.back: Glucose is the brain's only fuel; when levels drop, the brain panics and triggers emotional outbursts, confusion, even aggression — to push the person to find food fast.
basic.extra: Did you know: someone acting "hangry" may be a brain fighting to survive.

basic.back: Spasm or restriction of the jaw muscles causing limited mouth opening
Complete displacement of a tooth from its socket due to trauma
basic.extra: Often occurs during sports injuries, accidents or falls.

basic.front: Why is an avulsed primary (deciduous) tooth NOT replanted?
basic.back: Risk of damaging the permanent tooth germ.

basic.front: Why should a patient not spit, rinse, or use a straw on the day of a procedure that caused bleeding?
basic.back: Any suction can dislodge the clot and delay healing.
Loss of the clot after extraction, exposing the underlying bone and nerves — intense pain and delayed healing
basic.extra: Board Alert: a case mentioning a recent extraction = think: could this be a dry socket? Is the patient in pain? Do I need to prepare for a post-op emergency?

basic.back: Blood leaking into surrounding tissues after injury to a blood vessel wall

typein.question: Hypoglycemia = blood glucose below what value? (mg/dL)
Conscious hypoglycemic patient: how many grams of glucose do you give (repeated every 15 min)? (g)
Fluoride ingestion: above what dose does mild toxicity begin? (mg/kg)
typein.extra: The book also prints '10 mg/lb' here, but 5 mg/kg ≈ 2.3 mg/lb — learn the mg/kg values.

typein.question: A 15-kg child: how many mg of fluoride reach the 5 mg/kg toxicity threshold? (mg)
Failing to replant an avulsed tooth within the first how many minutes may give a less favorable prognosis? (minutes)
typein.extra: Book's figure. IADT 2020 guidance describes PDL cells as nonviable after more than 60 min dry time — either way, replant as fast as possible.

typein.question: Conscious choking infant: how many back blows per cycle?
Conscious choking infant: after the back blows, how many chest thrusts?
To prevent dry socket, avoid suction, spitting and smoking for at least how many hours post-op?
Seek emergency care for a nosebleed lasting more than how many minutes?
typein.extra: Also seek care if the nosebleed is related to an injury.

match.prompt: Match each fluoride dose to its management.
pairs: Milk (or substitute), induce vomiting, observe a few hours
EMS + hospital; oral calcium, induce vomiting
EMS + hospital; empty stomach, IV calcium gluconate, cardiac monitoring

order.prompt: Put the steps for reducing a dislocated mandible in order.
items: Brace the patient's head firmly against the headrest
Place protected thumbs on the mandibular occlusal surfaces, fingers around the ramus
Guide it up — condyle returns into the glenoid fossa

order.prompt: Rank avulsed-tooth storage options from best to worst.
Put the steps for a conscious choking infant in order.
items: Lay the infant face-down along your forearm, head supported
Deliver 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades
Turn the infant face-up, still supporting the head
Deliver 5 chest thrusts with 2 fingers just below the nipple line
Repeat until the object is expelled or the infant becomes unresponsive

sort.prompt: Choking: adult/child (over 1 year) or infant (under 1 year)?
Sort the drugs that raise bleeding risk.

mcq.question: A patient with diabetes skipped breakfast to make an early appointment. During scaling she becomes sweaty, shaky and irritable but is conscious and can swallow. What is the best first action?
options: B. Give 15 g of fast glucose such as juice
C. Call EMS and wait without giving anything
mcq.answer: B. Give 15 g of fast glucose such as juice
mcq.explanation: A conscious hypoglycemic patient gets 15 g glucose by mouth (juice or candy), repeated every 15 min. Glucagon 1 mg IM is for an UNCONSCIOUS patient; insulin would lower glucose further.

mcq.question: A patient with diabetes becomes unresponsive in the chair. You cannot tell whether it is hypo- or hyperglycemia. What is the most appropriate step?
options: A. Wait to see whether the patient recovers
C. Call EMS and give glucose
D. Place the patient upright and give oxygen only
mcq.answer: C. Call EMS and give glucose
mcq.explanation: Glucose can save a hypoglycemic patient and won't harm a hyperglycemic one short-term, so treat as hypoglycemia and call EMS. Insulin could kill a hypoglycemic patient.

mcq.question: A 20-kg child swallows about 200 mg of fluoride at home. What is the appropriate management?
options: A. Give milk and observe at home for a few hours
B. Activate EMS, admit to hospital, give calcium orally and induce vomiting
C. No treatment is needed below 15 mg/kg
D. Give water to dilute the fluoride
mcq.answer: B. Activate EMS, admit to hospital, give calcium orally and induce vomiting
mcq.explanation: 200 mg ÷ 20 kg = 10 mg/kg, in the 5–15 mg/kg range: EMS, hospital, oral calcium, induce vomiting. Milk and observation alone is for doses below 5 mg/kg.

mcq.question: Ten minutes after generous topical benzocaine, a 6-year-old has bluish lips and is short of breath. Cyanosis does not improve with oxygen. What is the most likely cause?
options: A. Local anesthetic overdose from intravascular injection
mcq.answer: B. Methemoglobinemia
mcq.explanation: Excess benzocaine (especially in children) causes methemoglobinemia — hemoglobin can't carry oxygen, so cyanosis persists despite oxygen. LA toxicity from injection presents with CNS signs first (metallic taste, tinnitus, tremors).

mcq.question: Right after an inferior alveolar nerve block, the patient reports a metallic taste, ringing in the ears and a numb tongue, then begins to tremble. What most likely happened?
options: C. Injection into a blood vessel (LA toxicity)
mcq.answer: C. Injection into a blood vessel (LA toxicity)
mcq.explanation: Metallic taste, tinnitus and tremors are CNS signs of local anesthetic toxicity, often from intravascular injection — prevented by aspirating. Methemoglobinemia follows topical benzocaine and shows cyanosis.

mcq.question: The day after a PSA block, a patient can open only about 2 finger-widths and chewing hurts. There is no fever or general stiffness. What do you recommend?
options: A. Ice packs and avoid moving the jaw for a week
B. Warm compresses, gentle jaw-stretching exercises, rest the jaw
C. Push the mandible down, back and up
mcq.answer: B. Warm compresses, gentle jaw-stretching exercises, rest the jaw
mcq.explanation: This is trismus: warm compresses, gentle stretching, rest, avoid wide opening. Down-back-up reduction is for a dislocated (stuck OPEN) mandible; tetanus is suspected only with fever and generalized stiffness.

mcq.question: A patient yawns widely during treatment and now cannot close her mouth. What is the correct management?
options: A. Apply warm compresses and wait
B. Push the mandible upward to close it
C. With protected thumbs on the occlusal surfaces, push the mandible down, then back and up
D. Have her bite on a bite block
mcq.answer: C. With protected thumbs on the occlusal surfaces, push the mandible down, then back and up
mcq.explanation: Dislocation = condyle forward past the articular eminence. Pushing straight up can't clear the eminence; press down first, then back and up into the glenoid fossa.

mcq.question: A 14-year-old's permanent central incisor is knocked out at soccer practice and you cannot replant it right away. No Save-A-Tooth is available. How should the tooth be transported?
options: A. Wrapped in a dry tissue
mcq.answer: C. In whole milk
mcq.explanation: Whole milk has an osmolality similar to root cells (good option). Water's very low osmolality ruptures cells, dry storage kills them, and skim milk is specifically not recommended.

mcq.question: A speck of debris enters a patient's eye during polishing. Which action is correct?
options: A. Rub the eye gently to dislodge it
B. Rinse with clean water from the outer corner toward the nose
C. Rinse with clean water from the inner (medial) corner to the outer (lateral) corner
D. Remove it with a cotton tip even if embedded
mcq.answer: C. Rinse with clean water from the inner (medial) corner to the outer (lateral) corner
mcq.explanation: Rinse medial → lateral so debris is flushed away from the other eye (avoids cross-contamination). Never rub the eye or try to remove an embedded object.

mcq.question: An 8-month-old in the waiting room suddenly cannot cry or breathe effectively and is turning blue. She is conscious. What should you do first?
options: B. Perform a blind finger sweep
C. Lay her face-down on your forearm and give 5 back blows
D. Tilt her head back and give rescue breaths
mcq.answer: C. Lay her face-down on your forearm and give 5 back blows
mcq.explanation: Infants (<1 year) get 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts. Abdominal thrusts are for over 1 year; blind sweeps are never done; the infant head stays neutral.

mcq.question: Two days after extraction of tooth #30, a patient who smokes calls with intense, worsening pain. What is the most likely cause?
mcq.answer: B. Dry socket (alveolar osteitis)
mcq.explanation: Dry socket peaks 1–3 days after extraction, especially lower molars; smoking is a risk factor. The lost clot exposes bone and nerves, causing intense pain.

mcq.question: A patient develops a nosebleed in the chair. Which instruction is correct?
options: A. Lie back with the head tilted back
B. Sit upright, lean forward and pinch the nose for 10 minutes
C. Blow the nose to clear clots, then pinch for 1 minute
D. Place the patient in Trendelenburg position
mcq.answer: B. Sit upright, lean forward and pinch the nose for 10 minutes
mcq.explanation: Upright and leaning forward lowers nasal venous pressure and keeps blood from being swallowed; pinch for 10 min. Tilting back or lowering the head sends blood down the throat or raises pressure.

mcq.question: Right after a PSA injection, the patient's cheek swells rapidly and turns bluish. What is the best management today?
options: A. Apply heat to speed resorption
B. Apply ice packs a few times a day
D. Push the mandible down and back
mcq.answer: B. Apply ice packs a few times a day
mcq.explanation: The needle likely punctured the pterygoid venous plexus. Day 1 = ice (vasoconstriction reduces bleeding and swelling); heat only from the next day. Aspirin would increase bleeding.

mcq.question: What is the compression-to-ventilation ratio for 2-rescuer CPR in children?
mcq.explanation: In 2-rescuer CPR for children and infants the ratio is 15:2. For single-rescuer CPR it's 30:2 for all age groups.

mcq.question: Which is NOT recommended during hyperventilation?
mcq.answer: A. Provide oxygen
mcq.explanation: Oxygen should NOT be given during hyperventilation — it worsens the condition by further reducing CO₂. The goal is to retain CO₂ to correct respiratory alkalosis.

mcq.question: A patient is experiencing chest pain. You administer nitroglycerin. When should you call 911?
options: C. After 1 dose with no relief
mcq.answer: C. After 1 dose with no relief
mcq.explanation: If the pain doesn't subside after the first nitroglycerin dose, assume it's a heart attack (MI) and call 911.

mcq.question: What is the appropriate action for a dislocated mandible during a dental procedure?
options: B. Push the jaw upward only
C. Push down and guide back into place
mcq.answer: C. Push down and guide back into place
mcq.explanation: To reduce a dislocated mandible, press down and then guide the jaw backward and upward to reposition the condyle.

mcq.question: In hypoglycemia, why does moodiness occur?
options: B. Brain uses amino acids instead of glucose
C. Brain is starved for fuel
mcq.answer: C. Brain is starved for fuel
mcq.explanation: The brain depends on glucose. When levels drop, the brain triggers emotional and survival responses like moodiness and irritability.

mcq.question: What is the emergency response for mild allergic reaction?
mcq.answer: C. Diphenhydramine
mcq.explanation: Mild allergic reactions are managed with antihistamines like diphenhydramine. Epinephrine is reserved for anaphylaxis.

mcq.question: In a seizure, which is NOT recommended?
options: A. Place tongue depressor in mouth
C. Let the seizure run its course
D. Turn patient to the side after seizure
mcq.answer: A. Place tongue depressor in mouth
mcq.explanation: Do NOT place anything in the patient's mouth during a seizure. Instead, clear the area and monitor until the episode ends.

mcq.question: A child is choking and cannot breathe. What is the first step?
mcq.answer: A. Deliver abdominal thrusts
mcq.explanation: If the child cannot breathe or speak, use the Heimlich maneuver (abdominal thrusts) to dislodge the object.

mcq.question: A patient reports fruity breath and excessive thirst. What is the likely emergency?
mcq.answer: C. Hyperglycemia
mcq.explanation: Fruity (acetone-like) breath is a sign of diabetic ketoacidosis, a complication of hyperglycemia when the body produces ketones due to lack of insulin.

mcq.question: What is the correct emergency step if a tooth is avulsed?
options: A. Scrub the root and replant
B. Hold by root and rinse with alcohol
C. Hold by crown and place in milk
D. Let it dry before replanting
mcq.answer: C. Hold by crown and place in milk
mcq.explanation: Always hold the tooth by the crown, never the root. Milk preserves periodontal ligament cells and helps increase replantation success.

mcq.question: Why is Trendelenburg position used in syncope?
mcq.answer: C. Increases brain perfusion
mcq.explanation: Raising the legs helps blood return to the brain, increasing oxygen and reversing cerebral hypoxia.

mcq.question: Why is aspirin dangerous during a hemorrhagic stroke?
mcq.answer: C. Increases bleeding
mcq.explanation: Aspirin inhibits platelet function. In a hemorrhagic stroke (where a vessel has burst), this could worsen the bleeding and lead to fatal outcomes.

mcq.question: What is the most appropriate position for a conscious asthma patient in distress?
mcq.answer: C. Upright
mcq.explanation: An upright position helps the patient use their diaphragm more effectively and improves airflow during an asthma attack.

mcq.question: Which of the following is the best reason to avoid using a straw after extraction?
mcq.answer: C. Dislodges blood clot
mcq.explanation: Suction from a straw can pull out the healing blood clot, leading to dry socket, a painful condition.
